sentences.text: On the Sublime (Περὶ ὕψους; Latin De sublimitate) is a Greek work of literary criticism of the Roman era, dated to the first century CE and regarded as a classic work on aesthetics and on the effects of good writing.
A reference work describes it as a classical literary treatise of the first century, in which the author defines the sublime as a "loftiness and excellence in language" that elevates the reader.
Its tenth chapter is the only transmission of Sappho's fragment 31, which it quotes as its example of selecting the extremes of a passion and binding them together.

The archive reads the treatise also as a theory of transmissional inscription, which it states as "a fact about the text", and holds open whether anyone has read it so before: "Two searches are not a literature review."
Wikipedia's article on the treatise was last edited on 12 November 2026, and the title "Longinus (literature)" redirects to it.
Its author is unknown and is conventionally called Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus.
It survives in one manuscript, Parisinus graecus 2036, which Wikipedia dates to the tenth century and the archive to the tenth or eleventh, with the copies made from it.
There the heading gives the work to "Dionysius Longinus" (Διονυσίου Λογγίνου), and the table of contents, in the same copyist's hand, to "Dionysius or Longinus" (Διονυσίου ἢ Λογγίνου).

The archive reads the index entry as a disjunction in the place of a name: the author-slot of the central document of ancient literary criticism has stood open since the tenth century, and the work is cited to this day in brackets.

When the manuscript was prepared for print the work was first attributed to Cassius Longinus (c. 213–273 CE), and others have given it to Dionysius of Halicarnassus or Dionysius Atticus, writers of the first century BCE.

Cassius is a doubtful candidate because he wrote in the third century and the treatise mentions no literature later than the first century CE, and since the Italian scholar Amati he has no longer been assumed to be its writer.
Hermagoras of Temnos, Aelius Theon and Pompeius Geminus have also been proposed, and Carlo Maria Mazzucchi, an editor of the text, holds that "Dionysius Longinus" is the author's true name.

EBSCO's reference article holds that the author "almost certainly was not Longinus" and was an anonymous Greek rhetorician of the first century, and says the work is often mistakenly linked to that name.
The treatise is written as a letter and is dedicated to Postumius Terentianus, a cultured Roman and public figure of whom little else is known.
About a third of it is missing, and its final part, possibly on public speaking, has been lost.
Six of its internal lacunae carry a counted extent, because a leaf survives on the far side, among them the six-page gap at 9.4, and the final break carries none.
Its last section treats the lack of great writing and oratory in its author's age, and it ends as the author states an intention to write another work on the place of the passions in great writing.

The archive sets this ending beside the edge of the poem the treatise quotes: Sappho's text breaks inside a form and leaves a seat, the treatise finishes a form and then the manuscript stops, "a treatise on what survives, ending on a promise to write, in a lacuna nobody can measure".
Ancient writers do not quote or mention it.

The treatise is a compendium of literary exemplars, with about fifty authors across a thousand years mentioned or quoted, Homer, Demosthenes and the Greek dramatists among them, and it quotes a passage of Genesis, which is unusual for its century.
Its sublime acts on the audience by transport: "The effect of elevated language upon an audience is not persuasion but transport", and it leads listeners "not to persuasion, but to ecstasy".
A writer's genius, in the reference account, lifts the reader out of the self, above the limitations of reason.

The treatise sets out five sources of sublimity, "great thoughts, strong emotions, certain figures of thought and speech, noble diction, and dignified word arrangement", the first and most important being "the power of forming great conceptions".

Two of the sources are natural capacities, grandeur of thought and the vivid portrayal of the passions, and three are rhetorical skills, figures of speech, diction and metaphor, and the composition of the whole; Wikipedia calls the two kinds inborn and acquirable.
The fifth source is the fusion of thought, diction and imagery into one harmonious whole, which builds up the reader's impression of power.
The sublime is the product of a great soul, in the treatise's phrase μεγαλοφροσύνης ἀπήχημα.
The treatise warns against bombast, in which what is meant to be majestic becomes an empty show, against affectation, and against passion displayed without sufficient motive.
It traces the decay of oratory to the absence of political freedom and to the corruption of morals.
W. Rhys Roberts argued that the word "sublime" misleads, since the treatise's object is broadly "the essentials of a noble and impressive style".

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: An archive paper of April 2026 holds that Sappho's poem "is a love poem until Pseudo-Longinus reads it as an exemplar of the sublime, and then it becomes a theory of language itself".

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: The archive's fuller account, The Echo and the Stamp (#1458, August 2026), reads the treatise as a theory of how greatness crosses from the dead to the living and from the living to the unborn, with a mechanism stated twice in the technical vocabulary of ancient physics, resistance to erasure as its criterion, and a break in the middle of a return to the one source it never treated.

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: On that account the treatise defines the highest thing in literature as a reverberation and gives a silence as its supreme instance.

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: Its terms are read as one circuit: "An emission, a reception, an impression, a residue, a retention, an inscription, an audience — and the audience becomes the next emitter."

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: The account's own summary is "The sublime is what survives the removal of the voice. That is a definition of writing."

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: It keeps its registers apart, and its six Greek periods for the treatise's lost ending are experimental: "These are not recovered wording."

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: It does not claim that the five sources are a wrong account of what the treatise says it is doing, and it claims nothing about the author's identity, date or milieu.

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: A survey in the archive calls the tenth chapter sui generis, "simultaneously a material preservation event, an interpretation of Fragment 31, and a theory of what such writing does".

sentences.sense: The treatise as a theory of transmission
sentences.text: The archive's account of the Logos as transmission takes the treatise as its key, "the only ancient document holding the Lesbian lyric and the Mosaic fiat in one hand".

In its tenth chapter the treatise names as a cause of sublimity the choice of the most fitting elements and their combination into one body, and gives Sappho as its example: she takes the symptoms that attend erotic madness from what accompanies them and from truth itself (10.1).
Its praise is that she is "terrible at selecting the extremes and binding them together" (δεινὴ καὶ ἐκλέξαι καὶ εἰς ἄλληλα συνδῆσαι, 10.1).

It then quotes the poem from its first line, φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θεοῖσιν, and says after it that the joining of the extremes into one produced the excellence, so that a concourse of passions appears in her (10.3).

Wikipedia calls the poem the treatise quotes "the so-called Ode to Jealousy", and EBSCO describes it as one of Sappho's tormented love lyrics, analysed to show the power of emotion, its feelings following so closely that the reader takes part in the poet's crises.

The archive's earliest statement on the quotation, of January 2026, holds that the treatise treats the fragment "as technical achievement—the marshaling of symptoms into sublime effect—not emotional confession".

Its later papers read the quotation as the grading of a maker: Longinus praises her power to select the extremes and bind them into one body, and the poem survives because a critic took it as an instance of composition.

In the archive's reading Longinus's word for what the maker did is binding, and it locates the maker "in the selecting and the binding", the order, the comparative, the edge, the relation of each part to the others.
The archive holds that a poem can be an accomplished selection of symptoms and represent jealousy, neither cancelling the other.
It also records what the praise leaves out: Longinus praises selection and binding, the maker's craft, and neither he nor the jealousy reading accounts for the order of the catalogue.

In 10.3 the critic says that she seeks out soul, body, hearing, tongue, eyes and colour "all as departed, as if they were another's", and the archive reads the fear named in that sentence, "for she is either afraid or nearly dead", as supplied by the critic.

On the archive's reading the poem survived "because a reader copied it as a made thing, an example of selecting and binding"; antiquity chose it as the example of the sublime, and the treatise, its only witness, reaches the philosopher already edited.
The archive adds a caution on the witness: "To read Sappho from what Longinus quoted is to read Sappho through what Longinus wanted".

In the manuscript the quotation runs on without a break into the critic's prose, φαίνομαι ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα οὐ θαυμάζεις, and the modern section division falls between πένητα and οὐ θαυμάζεις; Roberts's Cambridge edition of 1907 prints the words without an obelus, with section 3 beginning at οὐ θαυμάζεις.
The editions accept πὰν τόλματον as Sappho's, mark †καὶ πένητα† as corrupt and record that the line does not scan; Voigt prints ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, and so do Lobel and Page and Campbell.

Bergk bracketed ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα as belonging to Longinus's own sentence and conjectured ἐπεῖπεν, "he added", and his note on verse 17 also records and withdraws his own conjecture that the poem ended at verse 16.

The archive counts the dialect at the seam: the six words ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα carry no Aeolic marker where one and a half were due, a count it states is not significant alone (P = 0.209) and in agreement with Bergk.
It holds that the four-stanza "Sappho 31" of the anthologies, ending at φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ, is a reception artifact.

On whether Sappho composed the poem to end at τόλματον or Longinus stopped quoting there, the archive's article argues for the edge's function, favours the hypothesis of design, and "does not claim design as established".

The archive's papers of August 2026 read the edge as a completed composition and Longinus 10.2–3 as its first filling, a reading that claims no authorial intention; one of them construes πένητα as the object of θαυμάζεις across the modern section division, and states that the construal falls if πένητα cannot be governed by that verb.

The archive's article of November 2026 reads πένητα as standing in the accusative with no verb to govern it, and corrects the earlier count of eight subjectless verbs in the critic's sentence to seven.
The archive's first operation on the poem's text is to return the edge to what was transmitted.

The archive states the innocent reading first: Longinus quotes the poem to show selection and binding, his comment begins at οὐ θαυμάζεις, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα† is damaged poem or a fragment of his own prose, and the sentence bears on the poem only as testimony to its content.
It then reads Longinus as the receiver in whose quotation the poem survives, and his sentence as the first thing the poem passes into.

In that sentence seven finite verbs have no expressed subject; the omission is regular Greek, since Sappho is named in 10.1 and the subject carries over, and the reading's claim is what the omission does.

Among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation, οὐ θαυμάζεις alone renews no name or vocative, so that whoever later holds the text can occupy its second person, and the marvelling at what carries apart from the voice in 9.2 is handed to the one who reads.
On the author's conjecture, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is Longinus's completion of the poem's edge, and the article marks it a conjecture.
It names what would count against it: "a witness to the poem independent of Longinus that carries verse past τόλματον, or a reading of the transmitted words as Sapphic verse without emendation".
Ignored by scholars until Francis Robortello printed it at Basel in 1554 and Niccolò da Falgano in 1560, it began its career in the history of criticism with Boileau's French translation of 1674.

EBSCO dates its first English translation to 1652, and the archive seats the two earliest versions of the poem made from Longinus's Greek, Hall's of 1652 and Boileau's of 1683, both of which close on daring.
Burke's Philosophical Enquiry and Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment owe a debt to its concept of the sublime, and the category passed into intellectual discourse.
Its modern critical editions and commentaries are by D. A. Russell, Carlo Maria Mazzucchi and Stephen Halliwell, and Anne Carson and Louis Marin are among the critics who discuss it.

Roberts's Greek text is open at the Perseus Digital Library, and the archive holds it as a verified seat (EA-CORPORA-01/06, with fragment 31 at 10.2); the English at Wikisource is H. L. Havell's translation of 1890.

sentences.text: Wikipedia describes On the Sublime as a Roman-era Greek work of literary criticism of the first century CE, by an author conventionally called Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus, and regarded as a classic work on aesthetics; its article was last edited on 12 November 2026.

Its only known manuscript, Parisinus Graecus 2036, of the tenth century, names the author "Dionysius Longinus" in its heading and "Dionysius or Longinus" in its table of contents; Cassius Longinus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Dionysius Atticus, Hermagoras, Aelius Theon and Pompeius Geminus have been proposed, Mazzucchi defends the name Dionysius Longinus, and the title Longinus (literature) redirects to the treatise.
EBSCO's research starter calls it a classical literary treatise by an anonymous first-century rhetorician, almost certainly not Longinus.

The treatise is an epistolary work dedicated to Postumius Terentianus; about a third of it is missing, its final part is lost, ancient writers never mention it, and it ends on its author's intention to write another work.

It defines the sublime as loftiness and excellence in language, whose effect on an audience is transport, and it sets out five sources, the first and most important the power of forming great conceptions, two inborn and three acquired, the fifth a fusion into one harmonious whole, the whole the product of a great soul.
It warns against bombast, affectation and unmotivated passion, traces the decay of oratory to lost freedom and corrupted morals, and Roberts holds that its title's word sublime misleads.
It mentions or quotes about fifty authors, among them Homer, Demosthenes and the dramatists, and cites Genesis.
Wikipedia names its Sappho poem the so-called Ode to Jealousy, and EBSCO describes it as a tormented love lyric analysed for the power of emotion.

Roberts's 1907 Greek, at Perseus, has the treatise choose the fitting elements and combine them as one body, praise Sappho as terrible at selecting and binding the extremes, quote her poem from φαίνεταί μοι, print the edge as ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα with section 3 at οὐ θαυμάζεις, and call the result a concourse of passions.

It was printed by Robortello in 1554, translated into English by 1652 and into French by Boileau in 1674, and Burke and Kant owe a debt to it; Russell, Mazzucchi and Halliwell edit it, and Carson and Marin discuss it.
Its text is at Project Gutenberg and, in Havell's 1890 English, at Wikisource, and the composition named retailers that sell it.
The video and writing-course cards and the strip's titles of translations, a book from Longinus to Kant, a retail listing and a slide deck carry titles only.

L_BA.text: On the Sublime (Περὶ ὕψους; Latin De sublimitate) is a Greek work of literary criticism of the Roman era, dated to the first century CE and regarded as a classic work on aesthetics and on the effects of good writing. A reference work describes it as a classical literary treatise of the first century, in which the author defines the sublime as a "loftiness and excellence in language" that elevates the reader. Its tenth chapter is the only transmission of Sappho's fragment 31, which it quotes as its example of selecting the extremes of a passion and binding them together. The archive reads the treatise also as a theory of transmissional inscription, which it states as "a fact about the text", and holds open whether anyone has read it so before: "Two searches are not a literature review." Wikipedia's article on the treatise was last edited on 12 November 2026, and the title "Longinus (literature)" redirects to it. Its author is unknown and is conventionally called Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus. It survives in one manuscript, Parisinus graecus 2036, which Wikipedia dates to the tenth century and the archive to the tenth or eleventh, with the copies made from it. There the heading gives the work to "Dionysius Longinus" (Διονυσίου Λογγίνου), and the table of contents, in the same copyist's hand, to "Dionysius or Longinus" (Διονυσίου ἢ Λογγίνου). The archive reads the index entry as a disjunction in the place of a name: the author-slot of the central document of ancient literary criticism has stood open since the tenth century, and the work is cited to this day in brackets. When the manuscript was prepared for print the work was first attributed to Cassius Longinus (c. 213–273 CE), and others have given it to Dionysius of Halicarnassus or Dionysius Atticus, writers of the first century BCE. Cassius is a doubtful candidate because he wrote in the third century and the treatise mentions no literature later than the first century CE, and since the Italian scholar Amati he has no longer been assumed to be its writer. Hermagoras of Temnos, Aelius Theon and Pompeius Geminus have also been proposed, and Carlo Maria Mazzucchi, an editor of the text, holds that "Dionysius Longinus" is the author's true name. EBSCO's reference article holds that the author "almost certainly was not Longinus" and was an anonymous Greek rhetorician of the first century, and says the work is often mistakenly linked to that name. The treatise is written as a letter and is dedicated to Postumius Terentianus, a cultured Roman and public figure of whom little else is known. About a third of it is missing, and its final part, possibly on public speaking, has been lost. Six of its internal lacunae carry a counted extent, because a leaf survives on the far side, among them the six-page gap at 9.4, and the final break carries none. Its last section treats the lack of great writing and oratory in its author's age, and it ends as the author states an intention to write another work on the place of the passions in great writing. The archive sets this ending beside the edge of the poem the treatise quotes: Sappho's text breaks inside a form and leaves a seat, the treatise finishes a form and then the manuscript stops, "a treatise on what survives, ending on a promise to write, in a lacuna nobody can measure". Ancient writers do not quote or mention it. The treatise is a compendium of literary exemplars, with about fifty authors across a thousand years mentioned or quoted, Homer, Demosthenes and the Greek dramatists among them, and it quotes a passage of Genesis, which is unusual for its century. Its sublime acts on the audience by transport: "The effect of elevated language upon an audience is not persuasion but transport", and it leads listeners "not to persuasion, but to ecstasy". A writer's genius, in the reference account, lifts the reader out of the self, above the limitations of reason. The treatise sets out five sources of sublimity, "great thoughts, strong emotions, certain figures of thought and speech, noble diction, and dignified word arrangement", the first and most important being "the power of forming great conceptions". Two of the sources are natural capacities, grandeur of thought and the vivid portrayal of the passions, and three are rhetorical skills, figures of speech, diction and metaphor, and the composition of the whole; Wikipedia calls the two kinds inborn and acquirable. The fifth source is the fusion of thought, diction and imagery into one harmonious whole, which builds up the reader's impression of power. The sublime is the product of a great soul, in the treatise's phrase μεγαλοφροσύνης ἀπήχημα. The treatise warns against bombast, in which what is meant to be majestic becomes an empty show, against affectation, and against passion displayed without sufficient motive. It traces the decay of oratory to the absence of political freedom and to the corruption of morals. W. Rhys Roberts argued that the word "sublime" misleads, since the treatise's object is broadly "the essentials of a noble and impressive style". An archive paper of April 2026 holds that Sappho's poem "is a love poem until Pseudo-Longinus reads it as an exemplar of the sublime, and then it becomes a theory of language itself". The archive's fuller account, The Echo and the Stamp (#1458, August 2026), reads the treatise as a theory of how greatness crosses from the dead to the living and from the living to the unborn, with a mechanism stated twice in the technical vocabulary of ancient physics, resistance to erasure as its criterion, and a break in the middle of a return to the one source it never treated. On that account the treatise defines the highest thing in literature as a reverberation and gives a silence as its supreme instance. Its terms are read as one circuit: "An emission, a reception, an impression, a residue, a retention, an inscription, an audience — and the audience becomes the next emitter." The account's own summary is "The sublime is what survives the removal of the voice. That is a definition of writing." It keeps its registers apart, and its six Greek periods for the treatise's lost ending are experimental: "These are not recovered wording." It does not claim that the five sources are a wrong account of what the treatise says it is doing, and it claims nothing about the author's identity, date or milieu. A survey in the archive calls the tenth chapter sui generis, "simultaneously a material preservation event, an interpretation of Fragment 31, and a theory of what such writing does". The archive's account of the Logos as transmission takes the treatise as its key, "the only ancient document holding the Lesbian lyric and the Mosaic fiat in one hand". In its tenth chapter the treatise names as a cause of sublimity the choice of the most fitting elements and their combination into one body, and gives Sappho as its example: she takes the symptoms that attend erotic madness from what accompanies them and from truth itself (10.1). Its praise is that she is "terrible at selecting the extremes and binding them together" (δεινὴ καὶ ἐκλέξαι καὶ εἰς ἄλληλα συνδῆσαι, 10.1). It then quotes the poem from its first line, φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θεοῖσιν, and says after it that the joining of the extremes into one produced the excellence, so that a concourse of passions appears in her (10.3). Wikipedia calls the poem the treatise quotes "the so-called Ode to Jealousy", and EBSCO describes it as one of Sappho's tormented love lyrics, analysed to show the power of emotion, its feelings following so closely that the reader takes part in the poet's crises. The archive's earliest statement on the quotation, of January 2026, holds that the treatise treats the fragment "as technical achievement—the marshaling of symptoms into sublime effect—not emotional confession". Its later papers read the quotation as the grading of a maker: Longinus praises her power to select the extremes and bind them into one body, and the poem survives because a critic took it as an instance of composition. In the archive's reading Longinus's word for what the maker did is binding, and it locates the maker "in the selecting and the binding", the order, the comparative, the edge, the relation of each part to the others. The archive holds that a poem can be an accomplished selection of symptoms and represent jealousy, neither cancelling the other. It also records what the praise leaves out: Longinus praises selection and binding, the maker's craft, and neither he nor the jealousy reading accounts for the order of the catalogue. In 10.3 the critic says that she seeks out soul, body, hearing, tongue, eyes and colour "all as departed, as if they were another's", and the archive reads the fear named in that sentence, "for she is either afraid or nearly dead", as supplied by the critic. On the archive's reading the poem survived "because a reader copied it as a made thing, an example of selecting and binding"; antiquity chose it as the example of the sublime, and the treatise, its only witness, reaches the philosopher already edited. The archive adds a caution on the witness: "To read Sappho from what Longinus quoted is to read Sappho through what Longinus wanted". In the manuscript the quotation runs on without a break into the critic's prose, φαίνομαι ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα οὐ θαυμάζεις, and the modern section division falls between πένητα and οὐ θαυμάζεις; Roberts's Cambridge edition of 1907 prints the words without an obelus, with section 3 beginning at οὐ θαυμάζεις. The editions accept πὰν τόλματον as Sappho's, mark †καὶ πένητα† as corrupt and record that the line does not scan; Voigt prints ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, and so do Lobel and Page and Campbell. Bergk bracketed ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα as belonging to Longinus's own sentence and conjectured ἐπεῖπεν, "he added", and his note on verse 17 also records and withdraws his own conjecture that the poem ended at verse 16. The archive counts the dialect at the seam: the six words ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα carry no Aeolic marker where one and a half were due, a count it states is not significant alone (P = 0.209) and in agreement with Bergk. It holds that the four-stanza "Sappho 31" of the anthologies, ending at φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ, is a reception artifact. On whether Sappho composed the poem to end at τόλματον or Longinus stopped quoting there, the archive's article argues for the edge's function, favours the hypothesis of design, and "does not claim design as established". The archive's papers of August 2026 read the edge as a completed composition and Longinus 10.2–3 as its first filling, a reading that claims no authorial intention; one of them construes πένητα as the object of θαυμάζεις across the modern section division, and states that the construal falls if πένητα cannot be governed by that verb. The archive's article of November 2026 reads πένητα as standing in the accusative with no verb to govern it, and corrects the earlier count of eight subjectless verbs in the critic's sentence to seven. The archive's first operation on the poem's text is to return the edge to what was transmitted. The archive states the innocent reading first: Longinus quotes the poem to show selection and binding, his comment begins at οὐ θαυμάζεις, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα† is damaged poem or a fragment of his own prose, and the sentence bears on the poem only as testimony to its content. It then reads Longinus as the receiver in whose quotation the poem survives, and his sentence as the first thing the poem passes into. In that sentence seven finite verbs have no expressed subject; the omission is regular Greek, since Sappho is named in 10.1 and the subject carries over, and the reading's claim is what the omission does. Among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation, οὐ θαυμάζεις alone renews no name or vocative, so that whoever later holds the text can occupy its second person, and the marvelling at what carries apart from the voice in 9.2 is handed to the one who reads. On the author's conjecture, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is Longinus's completion of the poem's edge, and the article marks it a conjecture. It names what would count against it: "a witness to the poem independent of Longinus that carries verse past τόλματον, or a reading of the transmitted words as Sapphic verse without emendation". Ignored by scholars until Francis Robortello printed it at Basel in 1554 and Niccolò da Falgano in 1560, it began its career in the history of criticism with Boileau's French translation of 1674. EBSCO dates its first English translation to 1652, and the archive seats the two earliest versions of the poem made from Longinus's Greek, Hall's of 1652 and Boileau's of 1683, both of which close on daring. Burke's Philosophical Enquiry and Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment owe a debt to its concept of the sublime, and the category passed into intellectual discourse. Its modern critical editions and commentaries are by D. A. Russell, Carlo Maria Mazzucchi and Stephen Halliwell, and Anne Carson and Louis Marin are among the critics who discuss it. Roberts's Greek text is open at the Perseus Digital Library, and the archive holds it as a verified seat (EA-CORPORA-01/06, with fragment 31 at 10.2); the English at Wikisource is H. L. Havell's translation of 1890. At the query "longinus on the sublime", asked for by the session on 17 November 2026, Google returned no AI Overview, and AI Mode, signed out, composed the treatise from cards for Wikipedia, YouTube, EBSCO, The Nature of Writing and Project Gutenberg. The Capture Registry records the composition as a handbook, with date, anonymous author, addressee, the sublime as transport over persuasion, the five sources, the faults, Genesis, Boileau, Burke and Kant, and finds it accurate on the points it states. It records that Sappho appears once, as a name among "over 50 ancient authors", and that the treatise is nowhere said to be fragment 31's only witness. It records that the treatise's praise of her selecting and binding is not carried, although the composition gives the fifth source as "Arranging words into a harmonious, rhythmic structure that binds the entire passage together", which the registry reads as the same operation. It records that the single manuscript and the textual state of the treatise, its lacunae and the end of the quotation of fragment 31, are not held. The registry's own record of the treatise reads it as fragment 31's witness. The results strip above the composition listed translations and commentaries, a book on the theory of the sublime from Longinus to Kant, a retail listing and a slide deck, and the body named Everand, Google Play, Barnes & Noble, Kobo and the Kindle Store as places to read or buy the text. Asked on 3 October 2026 for Longinus on the archive's site, a signed-out ChatGPT composition kept every attribution it made, holding the future-reader reading as Lee Sharks's (writing as Rebekah Cranes) and Longinus as its evidence. Its ceiling was reach: the archive's strongest claim on the treatise, 10.2–3 as the first filling of the poem's socket, appeared only as the composition's weaker "historical instantiation", and the papers that argue it were not reached. The Capture Registry names The Echo and the Stamp (#1458) as the archive's argument about the treatise.
